name: Jesuit Refugee Service: advocacy and communication (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: the advocacy's value is humanitarian aid kept in the UN appeals, at the value of JRS's own programmes; spread like JRS's programmes in its southern regions by their 2025 expenses (Annual Report 2025, p. 33: Europe and North America left out, being outside the appeals), each region over its main country programmes by a judgment.
summary: The Jesuit Refugee Service's advocacy and communication ($4.4 million in 2025): pressing donors to keep refugee education and mental health inside shrinking humanitarian budgets, defending the 1951 Refugee Convention, asylum and detention work in Europe and the US, and public communication. It publishes no measured result, so it is built from ranged judgments and counted at half by the shared missing-data slider: JRS's share (0.4%, its southern regions' spending against the appeals' funding) of the aid that NGOs' funding advocacy kept, net of the aid it displaces, each dollar at the value of JRS's own programmes (charityevals' model, read live), plus a judged half again for its rights advocacy and communication. It comes to about 0.013 years of healthy life per $1,000 (combined range 0.0005-0.34), close to charityevals' NRC advocacy model, because JRS's share of the aid moved is small; the result is mostly uncertainty, driven by how much aid advocacy moves and JRS's part in it.

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What the modelled program cost in the year the outcomes below are counted for, including its share of overhead. From audited financial statements or the annual report.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: How many people, animals or meals the spending reached in the same year, as the charity reports it.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Value of a dollar moved (shared)
sections.explainer: charityevals' shared method for money a meta charity moves, the same rows in every such model (docs/normalization.md 2.8). A dollar moved is worth what the charities it reaches achieve, each at its live result on this site under your values; new money counts in full, shifted money only for the gain over where it would have gone.

sections.title: Career changes
sections.explainer: People the charity moves into high-impact jobs: per career changed, the pay they give up for the years they stay, valued at the new employer's live result per dollar, times the share of changes the charity caused (docs/normalization.md 2.8). The mirror of staff pay below market.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

Average yearly advocacy spending over the campaign's years, relative to 2025
rows.explainer: The funding kept comes from advocacy over the budget rounds behind it, set against the average real spending of those years over 2025's (estimate_basis past_average, Convention 11). rows.label: Humanitarian appeals funding received, 2025 (US$)

source.title: ALNAP, The State of the Humanitarian System 2026, 1.1 The reality of funding gaps
source.quote: Only 35% of the total 2025 appeals target was met.

rows.explainer: Funding received against the 2025 UN-coordinated appeals, 'to US$16.6 billion', against a shortfall of US$30.5 billion (same page, from OCHA's Financial Tracking Service); refugee response plans are part of it. Aid outside the appeals is left out, so aid per person is understated.

rows.label: Appeals funding per person in need, 2025 (US$)
rows.explainer: About $54.

rows.label: Money moved or raised for other charities in the year modelled (US$)
rows.explainer: JRS raises money for its own programmes (fundraising is overhead); the aid its advocacy keeps goes to UN agencies' and governments' responses, valued below, not to the site's moved-money destinations.

rows.label: Money moved per dollar of the charity's cost
rows.explainer: Context, and the donors' share of the resources with credit by share of resources on.

rows.label: Funding: share of a year's humanitarian funding kept or added by NGOs' collective funding advocacy
rows.explainer: Judgment 1% (0.2-4%), the same as charityevals' NRC advocacy model (one figure for the same question): donors' humanitarian aid fell 35.8% in 2025 (OECD, preliminary 2025 data, 9 April 2026, https://www.oecd.org/en/about/news/press-releases/2026/04/international-aid-fell-sharply-in-2025-says-oecd.html); NGOs' advocacy on the gap may have kept some budgets from falling further and kept education, mental health and protection inside what donors still fund, which is where JRS pushed (p. 26). 1% of 2025's funding is keeping about 2% of the cut: the cuts were driven by budget decisions advocacy barely moved.

rows.label: Funding: share of the money kept or added that comes from other aid
rows.explainer: Judgment 60% (30-90%): humanitarian budgets kept are partly taken from development aid within the same aid totals; the rest from donors' general spending. As NRC's and Save the Children's advocacy models.

rows.label: Aid kept, relative to JRS's programmes: counterfactual
rows.explainer: Judgment 1.19 (1-1.5): JRS's programmes are counted at the share others wouldn't have delivered, about 0.84 outcome-weighted (charityevals' JRS programmes model); aid added to the whole system isn't filled in by other responders, so a dollar of it is worth 1 ÷ 0.84 of JRS's, less where other money would follow. As NRC's advocacy model's 1.29 for NRC's 0.775.

rows.label: Aid kept, relative to JRS's programmes: what it buys
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.6 (0.25-1.5): JRS's value per dollar leans on education (over 90% of its value from 43% of its spending), while appeals funding goes mostly to food, health, shelter and logistics, which JRS's own emergency aid values at about a quarter of its average per dollar; health and nutrition work, which JRS barely does, is worth more per dollar. JRS's advocacy pushed for refugee education and mental health to stay funded (p. 26), so the aid it helped keep leans more to them than appeals funding as a whole: below NRC's 0.85 because JRS's average leans more on education.

rows.label: Value of a dollar of humanitarian aid, relative to a dollar of JRS's programmes
rows.explainer: The two parts above: about 0.7.

rows.label: Value of a dollar of humanitarian aid (units of value)
rows.explainer: charityevals' model of JRS's programmes, read live at your values, times the ratio above. The live read is that model's result at a missing-data discount of 1 (the engine reads models live that way), so the shared slider applies once, here, in missing_data_adj.

rows.label: Funding: value per person in need per year of the aid kept (units of value, before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Aid per person in need × the share kept by NGOs' advocacy × the share not taken from other aid × its value per dollar.

rows.label: Probability the change happens because of this work
rows.explainer: 1: the funding is reported as received in 2025; how much of it the advocacy kept is the share above, and JRS's part in it the attribution below.

rows.label: Years a won reform counts before it would have come anyway
rows.explainer: The site's shared years a won change counts ($win_years_counted, docs/normalization.md 2.9), capped at 1: a year's advocacy is set against a year's funding (the share of 2025's funding it kept), a flow; counting how long a kept budget line lasts on top would count a stock as a flow. As NRC's funding branch.

rows.label: Years from the win until the policy takes effect
rows.explainer: 0: the funding counted is what the appeals received in 2025, the year of the spending, so there is no wait to discount.

rows.label: Discount for the wait until the policy takes effect
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate, like every future benefit.

rows.label: Discounted years of impact
Expected value of the policy or research (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: People in need × value per person-year × years counted, discounted: a year's advocacy against a year's funding.

rows.label: Funding: value per year of advocacy at the average spending of the campaign's years
Other advocacy and communication, as a share of the funding branch's value
rows.explainer: The value of the line's other work as a share of the funding branch's value. Judgment 50% (0-150%): defending the 1951 Refugee Convention in a civil-society coalition, JRS Europe's and JRS USA's work on asylum and immigration detention, the position on local faith-based actors at the Global Refugee Forum review (p. 26), research on climate displacement (p. 29) and public communication against hostile narratives. JRS's advocacy leans more on refugee rights than NRC's (30%), whose voice is mostly on funding and access.

rows.label: Value of a dollar to global health and poverty charities (GiveWell's Top Charities, live), units of value
rows.explainer: GiveWell's four Top Charities (Against Malaria Foundation, Malaria Consortium's seasonal malaria chemoprevention, Helen Keller Intl's vitamin A, New Incentives), each at its result on this site under your values, weighted by what GiveWell directed to each in 2024 (50%, 29%, 18%, 4%).

rows.label: Value of a dollar moved, units of value
rows.explainer: This organisation moves money only to global health and poverty charities, so a dollar moved is valued at that destination alone (GiveWell's Top Charities, live).

rows.label: Value of a dollar where shifted money would otherwise have gone (our judgment: 1× GiveDirectly), units of value
rows.explainer: Our judgment. Shifted money was going to be given anyway; it is credited only for the gain. Where it would have gone is valued at GiveDirectly's live result (GiveWell's model), as Ambitious Impact does, times a shared multiple (1×, from 0 to 3×).

rows.label: Share of money moved that is new money
rows.explainer: The site's one figure for every meta charity: about half the money moved wouldn't otherwise have been given (Ambitious Impact's Effective Giving Incubation report), from 35% to 80%.

rows.label: Value of a dollar moved, net of where shifted money would have gone, units of value
rows.explainer: New money counts in full; shifted money counts for the gain over where it would have gone.

rows.label: Value of the money moved (units of value)
Evidence adjustment (internal and external validity), a multiplier
rows.explainer: 1: the funding total is measured, and what advocacy moved is a judgment already ranged in the share above; that nothing here is measured is the missing-data step's question, so no second discount.

rows.label: Share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 1: the share of funding kept above is already the difference the advocacy made (what would have happened anyway is netted out there, Convention 5).

rows.label: This charity's share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.4% (0.15-1.5%), anchored on a count as in NRC's advocacy model: JRS's southern regions, where its work is inside the UN appeals, spent $55.7m in 2025 (p. 33), about 0.34% of the $16.6bn the appeals received, a measure of its weight in the system (its $27.4m in Europe and North America is outside the appeals); its voice on refugee education and through the Catholic Church's networks is a little larger than its budget, but it advocates beside hundreds of NGOs and the UN's own appeals.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: Thin: the money kept and JRS's part are judgments with no measured result. So it is counted less by the shared slider, the same way in every model (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: All adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above.

rows.label: Units of value from JRS's advocacy and communication, per year at 2025's spending
rows.explainer: The funding branch with its adjustments, plus the other work's share; JRS's advocacy doesn't aim at career changes, so the template's career rows are left out rather than kept at 0 (their typed placeholder inputs would be a hand-copied house constant across five models, INV-14).

rows.label: Value per dollar
rows.explainer: For WELLBYs, rename the uov_* rows to wellbys_* and report in wellby. For animals, rename them to sads_* and add the species section of the corporate-campaign template (output ced_per_donor_dollar). For climate, start from the climate skeleton.
